newsitem.title: JAPAN: JAPAN INSURERS AT A LOSS TO SOLVE NISSAN LIFE CASE.
newsitem.headline: JAPAN INSURERS AT A LOSS TO SOLVE NISSAN LIFE CASE.

text.p: Japan's insurance industry is at a loss as to how to protect holders of Nissan Mutual Life Co's policies a month after the first failure of a life insurance firm in the nation's post-war history,

No candidates have presented themselves to set up a company to take over the policies, and without such a firm, the industry cannot use its Policyholders Protection Fund to protect investors, industry sources say.
The fund, to which 44 life insurers contribute, can inject up to 200 billion yen ($1.72 billion) into a company to take over policies from a failed life insurer.
If the industry fails to draw up a scheme to handle the Nissan Life failure, it will be handled under bankruptcy law, without any protectionary measures for policyholders.
This is something the industry wants to avoid.
"Nobody in the industry wants the case to be ruled under the bankruptcy law as it will severely hurt confidence in life insurers among ordinary people," an industry source said.
The sources said the current problem rose after Hitachi Ltd and Nissan Motor Co Ltd last week rejected a request by the Life Insurance Association of Japan to come to the aid of Nissan Life.
The association has been serving as an interim caretaker for Nissan Life since the firm was ordered by the Finance Ministry in late April not to take any new business because of massive debts.
A spokesman for Hitachi, a major client of the medium-sized insurer, said it was not in a position to bail out Nissan Life and had no intention of entering the insurance business.
A spokesman of Nissan, Nissan Life's second-largest client, echoed this view.

The life insurance industry had hoped the two leading Japanese companies would provide capital to a firm to take over Nissan Life's policies. Other life insurers have been loath to do so because they are still suffering in the aftermath of Japan's late-1980s bubble era, when many overextended themselves by offering excessively generous terms to policy holders.
The industry had also hoped Nissan Fire & Marine Insurance Co Ltd would set up a life insurance subsidiary to take over Nissan Life's assets.
However, a Nissan Fire & Marine spokesman said the firm would continue to focus on non-life insurance business.
Last month, a Finance Ministry official termed Nissan Life's financial situation "abnormal, with its liabilities exceeding assets by about 200 billion yen ($1.72 billion)".
However, industry sources said that a continuing inspection by the industry body had shown Nissan Life's actual liabilities exceed its assets by around 300 billion yen ($2.58 billion).
The Finance Ministry wants the industry to increase the total funds that would be injected into a new company from 200 billion yen ($1.72 billion), but sources said this was unlikely to happen.

"It's difficult to increase the (policyholders' protection) fund as each life insurer voluntarily agrees to provide money to the fund without any legal obligation," another industry source said. "It's a big amount for some financially weak insurers."
Nissan Life suffered heavy losses through excessive stock and real estate investment in the bubble era of inflated asset prices.
Nearly half of Nissan Life's assets are individual pension policies guaranteeing high returns, commitments that also damaged the company's financial stability.
The sources said that even if the industry could set up a company to take over Nissan Life's assets, policyholders would be asked to accept a cut in the high returns they have enjoyed.
They said it was impossible to continue paying out at the rates that have been promised up until the policies mature. ($1 = 116 yen)
